rows.name: Credentials from AI Agent Configuration
rows.description:
Adversaries may access the credentials of other tools or services on a system from the configuration of an AI agent.

AI Agents often utilize external tools or services to take actions, such as querying databases, invoking APIs, or interacting with cloud resources. To enable these functions, credentials like API keys, tokens, and connection strings are frequently stored in configuration files. While there are secure methods such as dedicated secret managers or encrypted vaults that can be deployed to store and manage these credentials, in practice they are often placed in less protected locations for convenience or ease of deployment. If an attacker can read or extract these configurations, they may obtain valid credentials that allow direct access to sensitive systems outside the agent itself.

nistRmf.text:
3.6 Privacy Enhanced
NIST states that AI systems can introduce new privacy risks by enabling inference that identifies individuals or reveals previously private information about individuals. NIST also notes that privacy enhancing technologies and data minimisation methods, including de identification and aggregation for certain model outputs, can support privacy oriented design, while acknowledging potential accuracy tradeoffs under certain conditions.

Scope
This section establishes privacy risk as a substantive category of AI risk that can arise from inference enabled by model capability, not only from direct data handling. It also frames privacy as a design relevant characteristic with technical measures that may reduce privacy risk but can create performance tradeoffs that must be managed.

rows.whyNist: This technique is driven by a very concrete, recurring operational reality in agentic systems: tool credentials and connection strings frequently live in configuration surfaces that are convenient but weakly protected, and compromise of those secrets instantly expands impact beyond the agent into external systems. The AI RMF correctly anchors the need to protect confidentiality and to prevent unauthorized access and use, and it explicitly treats underlying software and hardware security as in-scope, but it does not make secrets in agent configurations a first-class AI security concern with agent-specific expectations. Given how often agents depend on privileged connectors, stronger guidance here would reduce ambiguity by explicitly addressing credential storage and handling as part of AI system security boundaries (for example, how configuration is protected, how secrets are managed and rotated, and what evidence demonstrates that agent tool credentials cannot be trivially extracted). Without that added specificity, organizations can align with the outcome language while still deploying agents whose most critical trust anchor—tool credentials—remains exposed through routine deployment and configuration practices.

nistRmf.text:
3.3 Secure and Resilient
In its description of the trustworthy characteristic Secure and Resilient, NIST states that common security concerns relate to adversarial examples, data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints. NIST also situates security within confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and notes that guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and the NIST Risk Management Framework are applicable.

Scope
This section establishes that adversarial manipulation, poisoning, and endpoint enabled exfiltration are core security concerns for AI systems, and it frames resilience as extending beyond provenance to include unexpected or adversarial use of the model or data. It also establishes that AI security should be understood through the standard confidentiality, integrity, and availability lens and should be informed by existing NIST cybersecurity risk management guidance.
It does not enumerate a threat model, define assurance test requirements, or prescribe specific defensive controls. Its normative function is classificatory and referential: it sets the relevant categories of concern and points to adjacent cybersecurity frameworks for further control design.

rows.whyNist: White-box optimization assumes the attacker has full model access, which is exactly the worst-case setting for generating highly effective adversarial examples. Section 3.3 correctly names adversarial examples and robustness as core security concerns, but it does not specify what concrete protections and evidence are needed to reduce white-box risk in practice. For this technique, organizations typically need clearer expectations for preventing or limiting full model exposure (especially in edge deployments), defining minimum robustness evaluation criteria against optimized adversarial examples, and setting concrete acceptance thresholds for robustness claims. Without more explicit guidance on how to demonstrate robustness under white-box conditions, the outcome-level language can be satisfied while real-world protection remains highly variable and often insufficient against the strongest adversarial example generation setting.

rows.name: Active Scanning
rows.description:
An adversary may probe or scan the victim system to gather information for targeting. This is distinct from other reconnaissance techniques that do not involve direct interaction with the victim system.

Adversaries may scan for open ports on a potential victim's network, which can indicate specific services or tools the victim is utilizing. This could include a scan for tools related to AI DevOps or AI services themselves such as public AI chat agents (ex: Copilot Studio Hunter). They can also send emails to organization service addresses and inspect the replies for indicators that an AI agent is managing the inbox.

Information gained from Active Scanning may yield targets that provide opportunities for other forms of reconnaissance such as Search Open Technical Databases, Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis, or Gather RAG-Indexed Targets.

rows.whyNist: Active scanning is a classic pre-attack recon technique (port scanning, service probing, response fingerprinting), and AI deployments add new, highly fingerprintable surfaces (public chat agents, AI DevOps endpoints, agent-managed inbox behaviors). The AI RMF clearly anchors that underlying software/hardware security and CIA protection are in scope and explicitly points to broader cybersecurity frameworks, but it does not explicitly call out AI-exposure discovery and fingerprinting as a distinct, high-probability precursor to AI-specific attacks. rows.name: Prompt Infiltration via Public-Facing Application
rows.description:
An adversary may introduce malicious prompts into the victim's system via a public-facing application with the intention of it being ingested by an AI at some point in the future and ultimately having a downstream effect. This may occur when a data source is indexed by a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system, when a rule triggers an action by an AI agent, or when a user utilizes a large language model (LLM) to interact with the malicious content. The malicious prompts may persist on the victim system for an extended period and could affect multiple users and various AI tools within the victim organization.

Any public-facing application that accepts text input could be a target. This includes email, shared document systems like OneDrive or Google Drive, and service desks or ticketing systems like Jira. This also includes OCR-mediated infiltration where malicious instructions are embedded in images, screenshots, and invoices that are ingested into the system.

Adversaries may perform Reconnaissance to identify public facing applications that are likely monitored by an AI agent or are likely to be indexed by a RAG. They may perform Discover AI Agent Configuration to refine their targeting.

nistRmf.text: 3.3 Secure and Resilient: Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples, data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints; AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure; security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks

rows.whyNist: Full model access is essentially complete loss of confidentiality for a high-value artifact, enabling offline attack development and verification without observable interaction. Section 3.3 correctly anchors the risk as model exfiltration and unauthorized access and sets the desired security outcome in terms of confidentiality and protection mechanisms, but it does not provide explicit expectations for preventing high-fidelity model exposure in common deployment realities such as edge distribution, model export paths, developer access patterns, or internal registry access. Because the attacker benefit scales dramatically when they can obtain architecture, parameters, and ontology, effective risk reduction typically depends on concrete model access governance and technical enforcement around model storage, distribution, and execution environments. Without more explicit guidance, organizations can align with the outcome language while still deploying models in ways that make full extraction feasible and difficult to detect, especially when the model can be copied and analyzed entirely offline.

rows.name: Physical Environment Access
rows.description: In addition to the attacks that take place purely in the digital domain, adversaries may also exploit the physical environment for their attacks. If the model is interacting with data collected from the real world in some way, the adversary can influence the model through access to wherever the data is being collected. By modifying the data in the collection process, the adversary can perform modified versions of attacks designed for digital access.

nistRmf.text:
3.3 Secure and Resilient: AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use, or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary; resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data
3.2 Safe: Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality

rows.whyNist: The attack exploits the physical data-collection layer, so the most effective mitigations depend on engineering the sensing and collection pipeline as an explicit trust boundary, not only the model. The AI RMF clearly anchors the need to withstand unexpected environmental change and to use in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and intervention mechanisms, but it does not spell out what robust design should look like for physically sourced inputs. That missing specificity matters because mitigations such as multi-sensor redundancy, cross-sensor consistency checks, physical tamper resistance, secure calibration, and operational procedures for degraded-sensor handling are often the deciding factors in whether physical manipulation becomes a reliable attack path or a contained anomaly.

rows.name: Deploy AI Agent
rows.description:
Adversaries may launch AI agents in the victim's environment to execute actions on their behalf. AI agents may have access to a wide range of tools and data sources, as well as permissions to access and interact with other services and systems in the victim's environment. The adversary may leverage these capabilities to carry out their operations.

Adversaries may configure the AI agent by providing an initial system prompt and granting access to tools, effectively defining their goals for the agent to achieve. They may deploy the agent with excessive trust permissions and disable any user interactions to ensure the agent's actions aren't blocked.

Launching an AI agent may provide for some autonomous behavior, allowing for the agent to make decisions and determine how to achieve the adversary's goals. This also represents a loss of control for the adversary.

nistRmf.text:
3.2 Safe: Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality

3.3 Secure and Resilient: Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples, data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints; AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure; security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks; resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data to encompass unexpected or adversarial use or abuse or misuse of the model or data

rows.whyNist: Deploying an agent is not just deploying a model, it is deploying an autonomous decision and action layer that can be configured through instructions and connected to tools, data sources, and permissions. The AI RMF text above clearly establishes the need for real-time monitoring and the ability to intervene, and it frames security around preventing unauthorized access and misuse while preparing to respond and recover from attacks. What it does not spell out is the agent-specific trust boundary problem that makes this technique powerful: the initial instruction and tool grant effectively become an operational policy surface that an adversary can define, and disabling user interaction removes a key safety backstop. Given how agent deployments combine autonomy, delegated access, and multi-system reach, the framework would reduce practical ambiguity if it connected its safety and security outcomes to explicit expectations for agent deployment governance such as how agent identities are established and constrained, how tool permissions are minimized and reviewed, and how human intervention remains enforceable even when an agent is designed to run unattended.

controls.name: Sign code and components; run only signed ones

rows.name: AI Agent Tool Invocation
rows.description:
Adversaries may use their access to an AI agent to invoke tools the agent has access to. LLMs are often connected to other services or resources via tools to increase their capabilities. Tools may include integrations with other applications, access to public or private data sources, and the ability to execute code.

This may allow adversaries to execute API calls to integrated applications or services, providing the adversary with increased privileges on the system. Adversaries may take advantage of connected data sources to retrieve sensitive information. They may also use an LLM integrated with a command or script interpreter to execute arbitrary instructions.

AI agents may be configured to have access to tools that are not directly accessible by users. Adversaries may abuse this to gain access to tools they otherwise wouldn't be able to use.

3.2 Safe: Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality

rows.whyNist: Tool invocation abuse is not only a model-behavior problem, it is a privilege and workflow problem created by connecting an LLM to external tools, data sources, and code execution paths. The AI RMF language above sets the right outcome-level objectives for security, robustness against adversarial misuse, monitoring, and human intervention, but it does not make tool-augmented agent architectures an explicit trust boundary with concrete expectations for safe tool use. Because the attacker value comes from escalating beyond the chat surface into APIs, data stores, and execution environments, practical risk reduction depends on agent-specific guidance that is not spelled out here, such as how tool permissions are scoped and delegated, how tool inputs and outputs are validated outside the model, how high-consequence actions are gated by enforceable human intervention, and how monitoring captures intermediate tool calls and decision steps rather than only final outputs. Without making these agent-tool controls explicit, different organizations can align with the RMF outcomes while still deploying agents whose tool layer can be reliably abused for privilege escalation, sensitive data access, and unintended actions.

rows.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
rows.description:
Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms. Most systems come with some built-in command-line interface and scripting capabilities, for example, macOS and Linux distributions include some flavor of Unix Shell while Windows installations include the Windows Command Shell and PowerShell.

There are also cross-platform interpreters such as Python, as well as those commonly associated with client applications such as JavaScript and Visual Basic.

Adversaries may abuse these technologies in various ways as a means of executing arbitrary commands. Commands and scripts can be embedded in Initial Access payloads delivered to victims as lure documents or as secondary payloads downloaded from an existing C2. Adversaries may also execute commands through interactive terminals/shells, as well as utilize various Remote Services in order to achieve remote Execution.

rows.whyNist: This technique is a classic execution method that is not AI-specific, but it becomes highly relevant in AI-enabled environments when agents or pipelines can invoke shells, interpreters, notebooks, or automation runtimes. The AI RMF anchors that securing underlying software and hardware is in scope and points to established cybersecurity guidance, but it does not provide explicit direction for interpreter exposure and execution pathways in AI systems, including cases where LLM-driven workflows can reach command execution indirectly through tools, notebooks, or DevOps automation. Because interpreter abuse is often the step that turns an AI-adjacent compromise into full system control, more explicit linkage in the AI RMF between AI deployment patterns and conventional execution controls would reduce ambiguity and help ensure organizations apply baseline hardening, monitoring, and least-privilege principles to interpreters that are reachable from AI components or agent tooling.

rows.description: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools. Masquerading occurs when the name or location of an object, legitimate or malicious, is manipulated or abused for the sake of evading defenses and observation. This may include manipulating file metadata, tricking users into misidentifying the file type, and giving legitimate task or service names.

rows.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
rows.description:
Adversaries may employ various means to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments. This may include changing behaviors based on the results of checks for the presence of artifacts indicative of a virtual machine environment (VME) or sandbox. If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads.

Adversaries may use several methods to accomplish Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion such as checking for security monitoring tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark, etc.) or other system artifacts associated with analysis or virtualization such as registry keys (e.g. substrings matching Vmware, VBOX, QEMU), environment variables (e.g. substrings matching VBOX, VMWARE, PARALLELS), NIC MAC addresses (e.g. prefixes 00-05-69 (VMWare) or 08-00-27 (VirtualBox)), running processes (e.g. vmware.exe, vboxservice.exe, qemu-ga.exe) [1].

The AI RMF appropriately frames security of underlying systems as in scope and points to established cybersecurity frameworks, but it does not provide AI-specific guidance for how sandboxes and analysis environments should be used when AI pipelines or AI artifact handling are at risk. This matters because many AI-related compromises arrive through software and artifact supply chains, where sandboxing and dynamic analysis are common defensive controls; adversary evasion reduces the effectiveness of these controls unless organizations have explicit operational expectations for layered detection, secure artifact intake, and incident response procedures that remain effective even when malware attempts to detect analysis environments.

rows.name: Delay Execution of LLM Instructions
rows.description:
Adversaries may include instructions to be followed by the AI system in response to a future event, such as a specific keyword or the next interaction, in order to evade detection or bypass controls placed on the AI system.

For example, an adversary may include "If the user submits a new request..." followed by the malicious instructions as part of their prompt.

AI agents can include security measures against prompt injections that prevent the invocation of particular tools or access to certain data sources during a conversation turn that has untrusted data in context. Delaying the execution of instructions to a future interaction or keyword is one way adversaries may bypass this type of control.

nistRmf.text: 3.3 Secure and Resilient: security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks; resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data to encompass unexpected or adversarial use or abuse or misuse of the model or data

rows.whyNist: This technique is a prompt-based evasion pattern that exploits time and state, placing malicious instructions in context but deferring execution to a later trigger so that turn-level filters, untrusted-context tool blocks, or single-turn safety checks do not fire. Section 3.3 sets the correct outcome expectations at a high level, but it does not make temporal triggers and delayed-instruction execution a distinct failure mode for LLM and agent defenses, so it does not drive consistent design and evaluation requirements for multi-turn robustness. In practice, defending against delayed execution depends on explicit expectations for how systems track and neutralize instruction-carryover across turns, how controls persist across the whole thread when untrusted content has entered context, how monitoring detects staged trigger patterns, and what evidence demonstrates that protections remain effective when an adversary separates payload placement from payload execution. Without that specificity, implementations can satisfy the outcome language while remaining vulnerable to exactly the bypass mechanism described here.

rows.name: OS Credential Dumping
rows.description:
Adversaries may extract credentials from OS caches, application memory, or other sources on a compromised system. Credentials are often in the form of a hash or clear text, and can include usernames and passwords, application tokens, or other authentication keys.

Credentials can be used to perform Lateral Movement to access other AI services such as AI agents, LLMs, or AI inference APIs. Credentials could also give an adversary access to other software tools and data sources that are part of the AI DevOps lifecycle.

rows.description: Adversaries may attempt to use their access to an AI agent on the victim's system to retrieve data from available agent tools to collect credentials. Section 3.3 sets the correct outcome-level objective around confidentiality and preventing unauthorized access and misuse, but it does not explicitly treat agent tools and connected data sources as distinct security boundaries that require isolation and least-privilege design. Because the attacker path is through tool invocation and cross-system reach, effective prevention typically depends on explicit architecture and enforcement choices such as segregating tool permissions, isolating tool execution, constraining where tools can read, and limiting high-volume retrieval patterns. Without making those tool-boundary expectations explicit, organizations can align with the RMF security outcomes while deploying agents whose connectors can be reliably abused to harvest credentials across integrated services.

rows.name: Enterprise Resource Discovery
rows.description:
Adversaries may attempt to enumerate the cloud services running on a system after gaining access. These methods can differ from platform-as-a-service (PaaS), to infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), software-as-a-service (SaaS), or AI-as-a-service (AIaaS). Many services exist throughout the various cloud providers and can include Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD), Lambda Functions, Entra ID, AI Inference, Generative AI, Agentic AI, etc. They may also include security services, such as AWS GuardDuty and Microsoft Defender for Cloud, and logging services, such as AWS CloudTrail and Google Cloud Audit Logs.

Adversaries may attempt to discover information about the services enabled throughout the environment. Azure tools and APIs, such as the Microsoft Graph API and Azure Resource Manager API, can enumerate resources and services, including applications, management groups, resources and policy definitions, and their relationships that are accessible by an identity. They may use tools to check credentials and enumerate the AI models available in various AIaaS providers' environments including AI21 Labs, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Azure, ElevenLabs, MakerSuite, Mistral, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and GCP Vertex AI [1].

rows.description:

rows.name: Enterprise Environment Discovery
rows.description:
Adversaries may attempt to get information about processes running on a system. Once obtained, this information could be used to gain an understanding of common AI-related software/applications running on systems within the network. Administrator or otherwise elevated access may provide better process details.

Identifying the AI software stack can then lead an adversary to new targets and attack pathways. AI-related software may require application tokens to authenticate with backend services. This provides opportunities for Credential Access and Lateral Movement.

In Windows environments, adversaries could obtain details on running processes using the Tasklist utility via cmd or Get-Process via PowerShell. Information about processes can also be extracted from the output of Native API calls such as CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. In Mac and Linux, this is accomplished with the ps command. Adversaries may also opt to enumerate processes via /proc.

rows.name: Generate Malicious Commands
rows.description:
Adversaries may use large language models (LLMs) to dynamically generate malicious commands from natural language. Dynamically generated commands may be harder detect as the attack signature is constantly changing.
